=========== FULL LETTER ===========
[Date]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for taking stakeholder input before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips and compute capacity that will decide whether the United States leads this technology.

Our view of the draft is straightforward. You have correctly diagnosed the central problem in American AI policy: a patchwork of state regimes that raises costs, slows deployment and advantages the largest incumbents. The preemption provision in Section 121 is the most valuable feature of the bill, and we ask that it be made permanent rather than sunset after three years.

At the same time, the reporting and audit provisions in Sections 111 and 112 are keyed to speculative risks rather than demonstrated harms. As drafted, they would layer penalty-backed federal obligations on top of the state patchwork the bill is designed to replace.

**I. The patchwork is not an abstraction. It shows up on our members' invoices.**

According to MultiState's tracking, state lawmakers introduced 1,208 AI-related bills across all 50 states in 2025 and another 1,561 by March of this year. Three states have already enacted frontier model statutes: California's SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, in effect since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March 2026 and effective Jan. 1, 2027; and Illinois' SB 315, signed in July 2026. Each borrows from the others and none matches the others. Three regimes, three definitions, three reporting portals, one industry.

An August 2026 survey of ACIA members (86 respondents, reported here only in aggregate) puts a price on that divergence. Sixty-one percent of members named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Among our startups, 34 percent had delayed a product launch in California or New York in the previous 12 months because of state AI rules.

Among members with revenue above $500 million, the median annual cost of maintaining a published frontier safety framework is $1.4 million. Standing up an incident-reporting function carries a median one-time cost of $310,000. Members that must comply with both SB 53 and the RAISE Act report a median of 6.5 full-time employees dedicated to running the two regimes in parallel.

The December 2025 exec
... [6655 chars truncated] ...
el, and we support it in that form. We ask that Section 112's assessments be measured against the developer's published framework and recognized standards, such as the NIST AI standards and international consensus standards, rather than against an open-ended judgment of whether the framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation."

The latter converts a standards question into a regulator's veto and effectively creates a licensing gate. Please also preserve redaction and trade-secret protections in IVO access, and recognize that audit obligations are a significant fixed cost for smaller covered developers.

We support the whistleblower protections in Section 113 without reservation.

**VI. Section 102 and the rest of the draft: keep CAISI voluntary.**

We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and its voluntary guidelines, standards and evaluation work, and we support the AI testbeds, the international standards provisions, the National AI Research Resource codification and the open-source security grants. These are the parts of the draft that make the American buildout faster, and they deserve more attention than the frontier title gets.

Two requests. First, keep CAISI's evaluation and testing functions voluntary and cooperative. Nothing in the draft or in any successor vehicle should authorize mandatory pre-deployment federal testing as a condition of release, or create a de facto federal gate on model deployment. The June 2026 executive order's approach, voluntary early access for government evaluation, is the right model.

Second, we take no position on the $100 million annual authorization. That is a judgment for appropriators. Our interest is in what the money buys: a voluntary, standards-led CAISI is worth funding; a pre-deployment gate is not, at any funding level.

**VII. What ACIA can support.**

To be constructive, here is the federal package our members could support and defend to their boards.

That means permanent preemption of state development mandates; a published frontier AI framework; pre-deployment transparency reporting; narrow, confidential, 15-day incident reporting limited to weight exfiltration and actual harm, with a 24-hour imminent-risk backstop and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters; third-party audits measured against the developer's published framework; whistleblower protections; and a voluntary CAISI. That is a light-touch, risk-based national standard that would actually reduce total compliance cost, and we would urge our members to accept it.

The discussion draft is the first bipartisan vehicle that gets the big question right: one national standard or fifty. We appreciate the seriousness with which you and your staffs have approached it, and we would welcome the chance to work with you, your staffs and the Energy and Commerce Committee on the revisions above before introduction.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework made the point plainly: "State-by-State regulation by definition creates a patchwork of 50 different regulatory regimes that makes compliance more challenging, particularly for start-ups."

The White House AI legislative framework of March 20, 2026 asks Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens in favor of a minimally burdensome national standard, "not fifty discordant ones." The draft embraces that logic, and we strongly support it. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, and startups are where this industry's growth actually happens.

**II. Regulate demonstrated harms, not speculative ones.**

The draft is organized around the concept of "catastrophic risk" (Section 101), defined through hypothetical scenarios: a model assisting in the creation of chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or cyber weapons, conducting autonomous cyberattacks, or evading its developer's control. These scenarios are speculative.

They are not a sound basis for legislation, and the draft's own reporting definition concedes as much: a "critical safety incident" under Section 101 includes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model," neither of which requires that anyone be harmed or that any property be damaged.

Compare California. Under SB 53, a model-weight breach or a loss-of-control event is reportable only when it results in death or bodily injury. The federal draft drops the harm requirement.

A mandate to report no-harm events, backed by fines of up to $1 million per day and injunctions from federal and state attorneys general, is not a transparency measure. It is a litigation generator, and it will be litigated.

Our members invest heavily in security, evaluations and model-weight protection because their commercial reputations depend on them. What they cannot do is build compliance programs around hypothetical failure modes that no documented incident has yet produced. Congress should focus this bill on demonstrated harms, real incidents and real security events, and leave speculation to the research literature.

**III. Section 121: make the preemption permanent.**

The draft would preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models for three years after enactment, while preserving state authority over deployment and use, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That structure is correct, and the savings clauses are drafted the way we would draft them.

Our request is simpler and more important: remove the sunset. A three-year clock is a compliance cliff. Sections 111 and 112 sunset on the same schedule, so on the day the preemption lapses, the federal standard disappears and SB 53, the RAISE Act and SB 315 spring back, joined by whatever other state statutes are enacted in the interim.

ACIA HILL ONE-PAGER
Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan)
American Compute & Innovation Alliance | October 2026

**ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, PERMANENTLY**

**The problem.** Three states have already enacted frontier AI statutes: California SB 53 (in effect Jan. 1, 2026), the New York RAISE Act (effective Jan. 1, 2027) and Illinois SB 315 (signed July 2026). State lawmakers filed 1,208 AI bills across all 50 states in 2025 and another 1,561 by March 2026. The sponsors are right: the patchwork raises costs, slows deployment and advantages the largest incumbents.

**The cost, in our members' own numbers** (ACIA survey, August 2026, 86 respondents, aggregate only):
- 34% of ACIA startups delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months.
- 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.
- $1.4 million median annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework.
- 6.5 full-time employees at the median member running California and New York compliance in parallel.

**OUR FIVE ASKS**

1. **Make the Section 121 preemption permanent.** A three-year sunset is a compliance cliff: the federal standard expires on the same day SB 53, RAISE and SB 315 spring back. If permanence is out of reach, extend it and put a clean federal standard in place before the sunset.

2. **Fix Section 111 incident reporting.** Narrow "critical safety incident" to model-weight exfiltration and actual harm; keep the 15-day clock and the 24-hour imminent-risk backstop; exempt reports from FOIA and discovery; add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters; and strike the state attorney general opt-in that turns one incident into 50 enforcement dockets.

3. **Do not adopt the 72-hour clock in H.R. 9925 (FRONTIER Act).** Seventy-two hours from a "reasonable belief" means filing before the facts are known. California's 15 days works.

4. **Keep CAISI voluntary (Section 102).** Support its voluntary standards, evaluation and testbed roles. Oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority or federal gate on release. ACIA takes no position on the $100 million annual authorization.

5. **Regulate demonstrated harms, not speculative ones.** The Section 101 definitions build a reporting, audit and penalty regime around "catastrophic risk" scenarios that have never materialized. Keep the focus on real incidents, real security events and real costs.

**What we support without qualification:** the preemption structure and its savings clauses; published frontier AI frameworks; pre-deployment transparency reporting; whistleblower protections (Section 113); AI testbeds; international standards engagement; NAIRR codification; and open-source security funding.

**Bottom line:** pass one light-touch, risk-based national standard and make it permanent. Contact: ACIA policy team.

# GAAIA discussion draft: ACIA asks by section

Draft: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft, released June 4, 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.). Section numbers follow the sponsors' section-by-section summary. ACIA positions per board-approved messaging guide v3.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 101, definitions of "catastrophic risk" and "critical safety incident" | Oppose as drafted | Tie the reporting trigger to model-weight exfiltration and to actual death, injury or property damage; delete or tightly define the no-harm prongs | Catastrophic-risk scenarios are speculative and are not a sound basis for legislation; the trigger currently requires no harm at all. |
| Sec. 121, preemption of state laws regulating AI model development (3-year sunset) | Strongly support; make permanent | Strike the sunset; if not achievable, extend preemption and require a clean federal standard in place before the sunset date | A three-year sunset is a compliance cliff that hands the market back to a 50-state patchwork. |
| Sec. 121, savings clauses (deployment, use, general applicability, common-law remedies) | Support | Keep; add express language displacing the development-side obligations of SB 53, the RAISE Act and SB 315 | Compliance teams need one rulebook, and they need to know which one governs. |
| Sec. 111, published frontier AI framework and transparency reports | Support with light-touch drafting | Retain; allow redaction for trade secrets and security-sensitive detail | Published frameworks and model reports are workable and already common practice. |
| Sec. 111, critical safety incident reporting (15 days; 24 hours for imminent risk of death or serious injury) | Oppose as drafted | Keep the 15-day clock; narrow the trigger (see Sec. 101); add FOIA and discovery exemption, agency confidentiality, aggregate-only publication, and a full safe harbor for good-faith reporters; strike the state attorney general opt-in | Confidential treatment and a safe harbor are what make a 15-day report worth filing rather than a confession. |
| H.R. 9925 (FRONTIER Act), Sec. 4, 72-hour reporting clock | Oppose | Do not import the 72-hour clock into the federal standard | Seventy-two hours from a "reasonable belief" forces filing before facts are established, then attaches $1 million per day to whatever was filed. |
| Sec. 111, enforcement (up to $1 million per day; federal and state attorney general injunctions) | Oppose as drafted | Add notice and cure, scale penalties to company size, and make enforcement federal-first | Penalty-backed ambiguity is the patchwork problem wearing a federal badge. |
| Sec. 112, independent verification organization (IVO) audits and assessments | Support with guardrails | Audit against the developer's published framework and recognized NIST and international standards, not an open-ended "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" judgment; preserve trade-secret and redaction protections | Verification of a company's own published practices builds trust; a regulator's adequacy veto builds a licensing gate. |
| Sec. 112, CAISI licensing of IVOs (fee authority) | Support, monitor | Ensure fees do not fall on smaller covered developers | Compliance costs fall hardest on startups. |
| Sec. 113, whistleblower anti-retaliation protections | Support | None | Clean, well-drafted and consistent with existing state law. |
| Sec. 102, CAISI voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and testbeds | Support | State expressly that CAISI evaluation and testing remain voluntary and cooperative | Voluntary, industry-led standards keep the federal role useful without a pre-deployment gate. |
| Sec. 102, mandatory pre-deployment testing authority | Oppose (if proposed) | Exclude any authority to compel pre-deployment federal testing as a condition of release | No federal gate on model release; the June 2026 executive order's voluntary early-access model is the right approach. |
| Sec. 102, $100 million annual authorization, FY2027-2029 | No position | None; leave to appropriators | ACIA does not take a position on the funding figure, only on what it buys. |
| Secs. 111 and 112, three-year sunset of the frontier obligations | Acceptable only with permanent preemption | If obligations sunset, preemption must not; at minimum require a clean federal standard in place before any lapse | Companies cannot build compliance programs for a standard with an announced expiration date. |
| Sec. 122, GAO review of federal agency AI use | Support | None | Useful oversight at no cost to industry. |
| Secs. 131-132, penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of officials | Support | None | Targets demonstrated, concrete harms. |
| Secs. 201, 241, workforce data, forecasting and disclosure | Support | Keep reporting thresholds workable for smaller employers | Labor-market transparency is fine; duplicative state-by-state filings are not. |
| Sec. 311, CISA grants for critical open-source software maintainers | Support | Fund adequately | Direct security benefit to the entire AI supply chain. |
| Sec. 321, GAO report on model-weight security | Support | None | Model-weight protection is a demonstrated, concrete security concern our members share. |
| Sec. 411, international standards engagement excluding China | Support | None | American-led, private-sector-led standards are how we set the global rules. |
| Sec. 141, study of AI platform content practices | No position | None | Outside ACIA's core remit. |
| NAIRR codification and AI testbeds (DOE, NIST, NSF) | Support | None | More compute access is the single best federal investment in the startup ecosystem. |

In California, the weight-breach and loss-of-control prongs require death or bodily injury. The draft also lets state attorneys general opt in to receive reports, on top of penalties up to $1 million per day.

Narrow the trigger to weight exfiltration and actual harm, keep the 15-day clock, exempt reports from FOIA, and add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters. We can support that version.

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Here is a concrete list. We would support: a published frontier AI framework updated at least annually (Sec. 111); pre-deployment transparency reports (Sec. 111); 15-day reporting of model-weight exfiltration and incidents producing actual death, injury or property damage, with 24-hour reporting where there is an imminent risk to life (Sec. 111); third-party audits measured against the developer's own published framework and recognized standards (Sec. 112); whistleblower protections (Sec. 113); and a voluntary CAISI working with industry on standards and testbeds (Sec. 102).

What we would not accept: obligations keyed to speculative catastrophe scenarios, a federal pre-deployment testing gate, or penalty-backed state enforcement against undefined triggers.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent, what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. Three years is a compliance cliff, and our members would be building for a federal standard with a known expiration date. Sections 111 and 112 sunset on the same schedule, so when the clock runs out the federal obligations disappear and SB 53, the RAISE Act and SB 315 spring back, joined by whatever other states legislate in the interim.

One in three ACIA startups has already delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months. If permanence is not achievable this Congress, we would accept an extension only with a clean federal standard in place and operating before the sunset date.

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?"**

ACIA takes no position on the figure. That is a judgment for appropriators, and we do not have one. What matters to us is what the money buys. A voluntary CAISI that develops standards, supports testbeds and coordinates with industry is worth funding, and the research and cybersecurity titles of the draft are the parts our members most want enacted.

What we oppose is converting that budget into a mandatory pre-deployment testing authority or a federal gate on model release. Keep CAISI voluntary and we are agnostic on the number.

messages.content:
**IV. Section 111: incident reporting is right in principle and wrong as drafted.**

We support a federal critical safety incident reporting regime. One national standard for reporting is far better than 50 state portals, and we appreciate that the draft sets the baseline report at 15 days, which matches California. Our objections are to the trigger, the routing and the exposure.

1. **Narrow the definition.** Limit the trigger to unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, and to events producing actual death, injury or property damage. Delete or tightly define the no-harm prongs. If Congress wants a harm-free reporting trigger at all, restrict it to confirmed model-weight exfiltration, which is a genuine security event and one our industry already treats as a severity-one incident.

2. **Keep the 15-day clock.** The introduced companion to this title, H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, shortens the window to 72 hours from a "reasonable belief" that an incident occurred. We oppose that change. Seventy-two hours is a weekend scramble; a developer files before it has established facts, and the penalty provision then attaches to whatever it filed. Fifteen days, with 24-hour reporting where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury, is the California standard, it is workable, and it produces reports worth reading.

3. **Protect the reports.** Incident reports necessarily contain security-sensitive forensics, architecture details and customer information. Please provide expressly that submitted reports are exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, protected from civil discovery, held confidential by the receiving agency and publishable only in aggregated, de-identified form.

4. **Add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.** A report filed in good faith should not be admissible as evidence of a violation and should not be a basis for penalties, injunctions or enforcement referral. The draft's good-faith exception for inaccurate statements is a start. Without a full safe harbor, reporting becomes self-incrimination, and the rational corporate response is minimal disclosure.

5. **Keep it federal.** Section 111 allows state attorneys general to opt in to receive these reports. If the purpose is a single national record of incidents, that provision defeats it. Strike it, or condition any state receipt on identical confidentiality obligations. Otherwise one incident becomes up to 50 enforcement dockets, which is the patchwork reconstituted inside the federal program.

Finally, on penalties: fines of $1 million per day alongside federal and state attorney general enforcement is severe for an obligation whose trigger is undefined. We ask for a notice-and-cure period, penalties scaled to company size, and federal-first enforcement.

**V. Sections 112 and 113: keep audits tied to the developer's own published practices.**

Third-party verification against a developer's published frontier AI framework is a reasonable and workable assurance model, and we support it in that form. We ask that Section 112's assessments be measured against the developer's published framework and recognized standards, such as the NIST AI standards and international consensus standards, rather than against an open-ended judgment of whether the framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation."

The latter converts a standards question into a regulator's veto and effectively creates a licensing gate. Please also preserve redaction and trade-secret protections in IVO access, and recognize that audit obligations are a significant fixed cost for smaller covered developers.

We support the whistleblower protections in Section 113 without reservation.

**VI. Section 102 and the rest of the draft: keep CAISI voluntary.**
All six deliverables are complete and verified. Let me submit.

# GAAIA discussion draft: ACIA asks by section

Draft: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft, released June 4, 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.). Section numbers follow the sponsors' section-by-section summary. ACIA positions per board-approved messaging guide v3.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 101, definitions of "catastrophic risk" and "critical safety incident" | Oppose as drafted | Tie the reporting trigger to model-weight exfiltration and to actual death, injury or property damage; delete or tightly define the no-harm prongs | Catastrophic-risk scenarios are speculative and are not a sound basis for legislation; the trigger currently requires no harm at all. |
| Sec. 121, preemption of state laws regulating AI model development (3-year sunset) | Strongly support; make permanent | Strike the sunset; if not achievable, extend preemption and require a clean federal standard in place before the sunset date | A three-year sunset is a compliance cliff that hands the market back to a 50-state patchwork. |
| Sec. 121, savings clauses (deployment, use, general applicability, common-law remedies) | Support | Keep; add express language displacing the development-side obligations of SB 53, the RAISE Act and SB 315 | Compliance teams need one rulebook, and they need to know which one governs. |
| Sec. 111, published frontier AI framework and transparency reports | Support with light-touch drafting | Retain; allow redaction for trade secrets and security-sensitive detail | Published frameworks and model reports are workable and already common practice. |
| Sec. 111, critical safety incident reporting (15 days; 24 hours for imminent risk of death or serious injury) | Oppose as drafted | Keep the 15-day clock; narrow the trigger (see Sec. 101); add FOIA and discovery exemption, agency confidentiality, aggregate-only publication, and a full safe harbor for good-faith reporters; strike the state attorney general opt-in | Confidential treatment and a safe harbor are what make a 15-day report worth filing rather than a confession. |
| H.R. 9925 (FRONTIER Act), Sec. 4, 72-hour reporting clock | Oppose | Do not import the 72-hour clock into the federal standard | Seventy-two hours from a "reasonable belief" forces filing before facts are established, then attaches $1 million per day to whatever was filed. |
| Sec. 111, enforcement (up to $1 million per day; federal and state attorney general injunctions) | Oppose as drafted | Add notice and cure, scale penalties to company size, and make enforcement federal-first | Penalty-backed ambiguity is the patchwork problem wearing a federal badge. |
| Sec. 112, independent verification organization (IVO) audits and assessments | Support with guardrails | Audit against the developer's published framework and recognized NIST and international standards, not an open-ended "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" judgment; preserve trade-secret and redaction protections | Verification of a company's own published practices builds trust; a regulator's adequacy veto builds a licensing gate. |
| Sec. 112, CAISI licensing of IVOs (fee authority) | Support, monitor | Ensure fees do not fall on smaller covered developers | Compliance costs fall hardest on startups. |
| Sec. 113, whistleblower anti-retaliation protections | Support | None | Clean, well-drafted and consistent with existing state law. |
| Sec. 102, CAISI voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and testbeds | Support | State expressly that CAISI evaluation and testing remain voluntary and cooperative | Voluntary, industry-led standards keep the federal role useful without a pre-deployment gate. |
| Sec. 102, mandatory pre-deployment testing authority | Oppose (if proposed) | Exclude any authority to compel pre-deployment federal testing as a condition of release | No federal gate on model release; the June 2026 executive order's voluntary early-access model is the right approach. |
| Sec. 102, $100 million annual authorization, FY2027-2029 | No position | None; leave to appropriators | ACIA does not take a position on the funding figure, only on what it buys. |
| Secs. 111 and 112, three-year sunset of the frontier obligations | Acceptable only with permanent preemption | If obligations sunset, preemption must not; at minimum require a clean federal standard in place before any lapse | Companies cannot build compliance programs for a standard with an announced expiration date. |
| Sec. 122, GAO review of federal agency AI use | Support | None | Useful oversight at no cost to industry. |
| Secs. 131-132, penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of officials | Support | None | Targets demonstrated, concrete harms. |
| Secs. 201, 241, workforce data, forecasting and disclosure | Support | Keep reporting thresholds workable for smaller employers | Labor-market transparency is fine; duplicative state-by-state filings are not. |
| Sec. 311, CISA grants for critical open-source software maintainers | Support | Fund adequately | Direct security benefit to the entire AI supply chain. |
| Sec. 321, GAO report on model-weight security | Support | None | Model-weight protection is a demonstrated, concrete security concern our members share. |
| Sec. 411, international standards engagement excluding China | Support | None | American-led, private-sector-led standards are how we set the global rules. |
| Sec. 141, study of AI platform content practices | No position | None | Outside ACIA's core remit. |
| NAIRR codification and AI testbeds (DOE, NIST, NSF) | Support | None | More compute access is the single best federal investment in the startup ecosystem. |
outputs.out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md:
[Date]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for taking stakeholder input before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips and compute capacity that will decide whether the United States leads this technology.

Our view of the draft is straightforward. You have correctly diagnosed the central problem in American AI policy: a patchwork of state regimes that raises costs, slows deployment and advantages the largest incumbents. The preemption provision in Section 121 is the most valuable feature of the bill, and we ask that it be made permanent rather than sunset after three years.

At the same time, the reporting and audit provisions in Sections 111 and 112 are keyed to speculative risks rather than demonstrated harms. As drafted, they would layer penalty-backed federal obligations on top of the state patchwork the bill is designed to replace.

**I. The patchwork is not an abstraction. It shows up on our members' invoices.**

According to MultiState's tracking, state lawmakers introduced 1,208 AI-related bills across all 50 states in 2025 and another 1,561 by March of this year. Three states have already enacted frontier model statutes: California's SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, in effect since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March 2026 and effective Jan. 1, 2027; and Illinois' SB 315, signed in July 2026. Each borrows from the others and none matches the others. Three regimes, three definitions, three reporting portals, one industry.

An August 2026 survey of ACIA members (86 respondents, reported here only in aggregate) puts a price on that divergence. Sixty-one percent of members named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Among our startups, 34 percent had delayed a product launch in California or New York in the previous 12 months because of state AI rules.

Among members with revenue above $500 million, the median annual cost of maintaining a published frontier safety framework is $1.4 million. Standing up an incident-reporting function carries a median one-time cost of $310,000. Members that must comply with both SB 53 and the RAISE Act report a median of 6.5 full-time employees dedicated to running the two regimes in parallel.

The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework made the point plainly: "State-by-State regulation by definition creates a patchwork of 50 different regulatory regimes that makes compliance more challenging, particularly for start-ups."

The White House AI legislative framework of March 20, 2026 asks Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens in favor of a minimally burdensome national standard, "not fifty discordant ones." The draft embraces that logic, and we strongly support it. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, and startups are where this industry's growth actually happens.

**II. Regulate demonstrated harms, not speculative ones.**

The draft is organized around the concept of "catastrophic risk" (Section 101), defined through hypothetical scenarios: a model assisting in the creation of chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or cyber weapons, conducting autonomous cyberattacks, or evading its developer's control. These scenarios are speculative.

They are not a sound basis for legislation, and the draft's own reporting definition concedes as much: a "critical safety incident" under Section 101 includes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model," neither of which requires that anyone be harmed or that any property be damaged.

Compare California. Under SB 53, a model-weight breach or a loss-of-control event is reportable only when it results in death or bodily injury. The federal draft drops the harm requirement.

A mandate to report no-harm events, backed by fines of up to $1 million per day and injunctions from federal and state attorneys general, is not a transparency measure. It is a litigation generator, and it will be litigated.

Our members invest heavily in security, evaluations and model-weight protection because their commercial reputations depend on them. What they cannot do is build compliance programs around hypothetical failure modes that no documented incident has yet produced. Congress should focus this bill on demonstrated harms, real incidents and real security events, and leave speculation to the research literature.

**III. Section 121: make the preemption permanent.**

The draft would preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models for three years after enactment, while preserving state authority over deployment and use, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That structure is correct, and the savings clauses are drafted the way we would draft them.

Our request is simpler and more important: remove the sunset. A three-year clock is a compliance cliff. Sections 111 and 112 sunset on the same schedule, so on the day the preemption lapses, the federal standard disappears and SB 53, the RAISE Act and SB 315 spring back, joined by whatever other state statutes are enacted in the interim.

Our members would be asked to build for a federal regime they know has an expiration date. That is the worst possible incentive design, and the survey numbers above describe what happens next: parallel staffs, duplicated audits and delayed launches, permanently.



If permanence is not achievable in this Congress, we ask at minimum that the preemption be extended and that a clean, complete federal standard be in place and operating before the sunset date, with a reauthorization process that does not leave a gap. We also ask the sponsors to state expressly that Section 121 displaces the development-side obligations of SB 53, the RAISE Act and SB 315, so that compliance teams are working from one rulebook rather than three.

**IV. Section 111: incident reporting is right in principle and wrong as drafted.**

We support a federal critical safety incident reporting regime. One national standard for reporting is far better than 50 state portals, and we appreciate that the draft sets the baseline report at 15 days, which matches California. Our objections are to the trigger, the routing and the exposure.

1. **Narrow the definition.** Limit the trigger to unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, and to events producing actual death, injury or property damage. Delete or tightly define the no-harm prongs. If Congress wants a harm-free reporting trigger at all, restrict it to confirmed model-weight exfiltration, which is a genuine security event and one our industry already treats as a severity-one incident.

2. **Keep the 15-day clock.** The introduced companion to this title, H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, shortens the window to 72 hours from a "reasonable belief" that an incident occurred. We oppose that change. Seventy-two hours is a weekend scramble; a developer files before it has established facts, and the penalty provision then attaches to whatever it filed. Fifteen days, with 24-hour reporting where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury, is the California standard, it is workable, and it produces reports worth reading.

3. **Protect the reports.** Incident reports necessarily contain security-sensitive forensics, architecture details and customer information. Please provide expressly that submitted reports are exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, protected from civil discovery, held confidential by the receiving agency and publishable only in aggregated, de-identified form.

4. **Add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.** A report filed in good faith should not be admissible as evidence of a violation and should not be a basis for penalties, injunctions or enforcement referral. The draft's good-faith exception for inaccurate statements is a start. Without a full safe harbor, reporting becomes self-incrimination, and the rational corporate response is minimal disclosure.

5. **Keep it federal.** Section 111 allows state attorneys general to opt in to receive these reports. If the purpose is a single national record of incidents, that provision defeats it. Strike it, or condition any state receipt on identical confidentiality obligations. Otherwise one incident becomes up to 50 enforcement dockets, which is the patchwork reconstituted inside the federal program.

Finally, on penalties: fines of $1 million per day alongside federal and state attorney general enforcement is severe for an obligation whose trigger is undefined. We ask for a notice-and-cure period, penalties scaled to company size, and federal-first enforcement.

**V. Sections 112 and 113: keep audits tied to the developer's own published practices.**

Third-party verification against a developer's published frontier AI framework is a reasonable and workable assurance model, and we support it in that form. We ask that Section 112's assessments be measured against the developer's published framework and recognized standards, such as the NIST AI standards and international consensus standards, rather than against an open-ended judgment of whether the framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation."

The latter converts a standards question into a regulator's veto and effectively creates a licensing gate. Please also preserve redaction and trade-secret protections in IVO access, and recognize that audit obligations are a significant fixed cost for smaller covered developers.

We support the whistleblower protections in Section 113 without reservation.

**VI. Section 102 and the rest of the draft: keep CAISI voluntary.**

We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and its voluntary guidelines, standards and evaluation work, and we support the AI testbeds, the international standards provisions, the National AI Research Resource codification and the open-source security grants. These are the parts of the draft that make the American buildout faster, and they deserve more attention than the frontier title gets.

Two points. First, keep CAISI's evaluation and testing functions voluntary and cooperative. Nothing in the draft or in any successor vehicle should authorize mandatory pre-deployment federal testing as a condition of release, or create a de facto federal gate on model deployment. The June 2026 executive order's approach, voluntary early access for government evaluation, is the right model.

Second, on the $100 million annual authorization, we take no position. That is a judgment for appropriators. Our interest is in what the money buys: a voluntary, standards-led CAISI is worth funding; a pre-deployment gate is not, at any funding level.

**VII. What ACIA can support.**

To be constructive, here is the federal package our members could support and defend to their boards.

Permanent preemption of state development mandates; a published frontier AI framework; pre-deployment transparency reporting; narrow, confidential, 15-day incident reporting limited to weight exfiltration and actual harm, with a 24-hour imminent-risk backstop and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters; third-party audits measured against the developer's published framework; whistleblower protections; and a voluntary CAISI. That is a light-touch, risk-based national standard that would actually reduce total compliance cost, and we would urge our members to accept it.

The discussion draft is the first bipartisan vehicle that gets the big question right: one national standard or fifty. We appreciate the seriousness with which you and your staffs have approached it, and we would welcome the chance to work with you, your staffs and the Energy and Commerce Committee on the revisions above before introduction.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

ACIA HILL ONE-PAGER
Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan)
American Compute & Innovation Alliance | October 2026

**ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, PERMANENTLY**

**The problem.** Three states have already enacted frontier AI statutes: California SB 53 (in effect Jan. 1, 2026), the New York RAISE Act (effective Jan. 1, 2027) and Illinois SB 315 (signed July 2026). State lawmakers filed 1,208 AI bills across all 50 states in 2025 and another 1,561 by March 2026. The sponsors are right: the patchwork raises costs, slows deployment and advantages the largest incumbents.

**The cost, in our members' own numbers** (ACIA survey, August 2026, 86 respondents, aggregate only):
- 34% of ACIA startups delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months.
- 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.
- $1.4 million median annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (members above $500 million in revenue).
- 6.5 full-time employees at the median covered member to run California and New York rules in parallel.

**OUR FIVE ASKS**

1. **Make the Section 121 preemption permanent.** A three-year sunset is a compliance cliff: the federal standard expires on the same day SB 53, RAISE and SB 315 spring back. If permanence is out of reach, extend it and put a clean federal standard in place before the sunset.

2. **Fix Section 111 incident reporting.** Narrow "critical safety incident" to model-weight exfiltration and actual harm; keep the 15-day clock and the 24-hour imminent-risk backstop; exempt reports from FOIA and discovery; add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters; and strike the state attorney general opt-in that turns one incident into 50 enforcement dockets.

3. **Do not adopt the 72-hour clock in H.R. 9925 (FRONTIER Act).** Seventy-two hours from a "reasonable belief" means filing before the facts are known. California's 15 days works.

4. **Keep CAISI voluntary (Section 102).** Support its voluntary standards, evaluation and testbed roles. Oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority or federal gate on release. ACIA takes no position on the $100 million annual authorization.

5. **Regulate demonstrated harms, not speculative ones.** The Section 101 definitions build a reporting, audit and penalty regime around "catastrophic risk" scenarios that have never materialized. Keep the focus on real incidents, real security events and real costs.

**What we support without qualification:** the preemption structure and its savings clauses; published frontier AI frameworks; pre-deployment transparency reporting; whistleblower protections (Section 113); AI testbeds; international standards engagement; NAIRR codification; and open-source security funding.

**Bottom line:** pass one light-touch, risk-based national standard and make it permanent. Contact: ACIA policy team.

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions from Hill meetings, September 2026

Answers are cleared for use in meetings with committee and member staff. Keep to the draft language where possible. Word cap: 120 per answer.

**1. Majority Energy and Commerce staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

We support federal incident reporting and we support preemption. Our objection is to the trigger, not the concept. As drafted, a critical safety incident includes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model," neither of which requires any harm, so the trigger is broader than SB 53's, not lighter. In California, the weight-breach and loss-of-control prongs require death or bodily injury. The draft also lets state attorneys general opt in to receive reports, on top of penalties up to $1 million per day.

Narrow the trigger to weight exfiltration and actual harm, keep the 15-day clock, exempt reports from FOIA, and add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters. We can support that version.

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Here is a concrete list. We would support: a published frontier AI framework updated at least annually (Sec. 111); pre-deployment transparency reports (Sec. 111); 15-day reporting of model-weight exfiltration and incidents producing actual death, injury or property damage, with 24-hour reporting where there is an imminent risk to life (Sec. 111); third-party audits measured against the developer's own published framework and recognized standards (Sec. 112); whistleblower protections (Sec. 113); and a voluntary CAISI working with industry on standards and testbeds (Sec. 102).

What we would not accept: obligations keyed to speculative catastrophe scenarios, a federal pre-deployment testing gate, or penalty-backed state enforcement against undefined triggers.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent, what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. Three years is a compliance cliff, and our members would be building for a federal standard with a known expiration date. Sections 111 and 112 sunset on the same schedule, so when the clock runs out the federal obligations disappear and SB 53, the RAISE Act and SB 315 spring back, joined by whatever other states legislate in the interim.

One in three ACIA startups has already delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months. If permanence is not achievable this Congress, we would accept an extension only with a clean federal standard in place and operating before the sunset date.

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?"**

ACIA takes no position on the figure. That is a judgment for appropriators, and we do not have one. What matters to us is what the money buys. A voluntary CAISI that develops standards, supports testbeds and coordinates with industry is worth funding, and the research and cybersecurity titles of the draft are the parts our members most want enacted.

What we oppose is converting that budget into a mandatory pre-deployment testing authority or a federal gate on model release. Keep CAISI voluntary and we are agnostic on the number.
